resources.string: Habit and relationship
Fruit and seed
Pedunculate oak
Quercus robur
Chêne pédonculé
Very short leaf stalk with small basal lobes. Acorns on long stalks. The two oaks can hybridise: examine several features.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sessile oak
Quercus petraea
Chêne sessile
Well-developed leaf stalk; leaf base usually wedge-shaped without pronounced basal lobes. Acorns nearly stalkless on the twig. Intermediate forms occur.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Norway maple
Acer platanoides
Érable plane
Leaf lobes end in long points. Upright flower clusters, often before the leaves. Samara wings form a very wide angle.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sycamore maple
Acer pseudoplatanus
Érable sycomore
Large five-lobed toothed leaves. Flowers in hanging racemes. Samara wings are closer together than in Norway maple; older bark flakes in plates.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Wild cherry
Prunus avium
Merisier
Toothed leaves, often with two red glands on the stalk. Bark with horizontal lenticels. White flowers in small clusters; long-stalked cherries.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European aspen
Populus tremula
Peuplier tremble
Rounded mature leaves with long flattened stalks that flutter in the wind. Young shoot leaves may be more triangular. Catkins precede the leaves; seeds have cottony hairs.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Scots pine
Pinus sylvestris
Pin sylvestre
Needles in pairs, slightly twisted. Upper trunk often orange. Egg-shaped cones with woody scales mature over more than one season.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Norway spruce
Picea abies
Épicéa commun
Sharp four-sided needles attached all around the twig on small pegs. Long hanging cones fall intact.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
European larch
Larix decidua
Mélèze d’Europe
Soft needles in tufts on short shoots, single on long shoots. Needles turn yellow and fall in autumn. Small upright cones remain on the branches.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Dog rose
Rosa canina
Églantier
Arching stems with hooked prickles. Leaves usually have 5–7 leaflets. Five-petalled flowers; red hips contain the small dry fruits. The dog-rose group is complex.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common holly
Ilex aquifolium
Houx commun
Thick glossy leaves, often spiny low down but sometimes entire higher up. Male and female flowers usually occur on separate plants. Red fruits on female plants.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Wild privet
Ligustrum vulgare
Troène commun
Opposite entire leaves, sometimes retained through part of winter. Tiny white four-lobed flowers in terminal panicles. Black fruits; leaf retention depends on climate.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Oxeye daisy
Leucanthemum vulgare
Marguerite commune
Stems bear alternate leaves; basal leaves are broader than upper leaves. Large white-and-yellow flower heads. Several related oxeye daisies require detailed examination.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common poppy
Papaver rhoeas
Coquelicot
Stem with spreading hairs and a nodding flower bud. Four crumpled red petals, sometimes black at the base. Rounded capsule topped by a radiating disc and opening through pores.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Meadow buttercup
Ranunculus acris
Renoncule âcre
Leaves deeply divided into narrow segments. Upright flowers have five glossy yellow petals and many stamens. Small achenes form a head; several buttercups look alike.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cowslip
Primula veris
Primevère officinale
Rosette of wrinkled leaves. A stalk bears several flowers nodding to one side; yellow corollas with small orange marks and inflated pale calyces.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common bird’s-foot trefoil
Lotus corniculatus
Lotier corniculé
Five leaflets: three at the tip and two near the base. Small clusters of yellow, sometimes orange-tinted flowers. Slender pods spread like toes.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Ribwort plantain
Plantago lanceolata
Plantain lancéolé
Rosette of narrow leaves with 3–5 prominent lengthwise veins. Grooved leafless stalk ends in a short spike ringed by pale stamens during flowering.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Greater plantain
Plantago major
Grand plantain
Rosette of broad oval leaves with long stalks and strong curved veins. Long slender spikes of inconspicuous flowers. Common on compacted ground and paths.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
White dead-nettle
Lamium album
Lamier blanc
Opposite toothed nettle-like leaves without stinging hairs. Square stem. Large white two-lipped flowers cluster around the stem at the nodes.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Perennial ryegrass
Lolium perenne
Ivraie vivace
Leaves often glossy underneath. Simple spike: alternate spikelets are set edge-on to the axis. Usually awnless; small auricles clasp the stem.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Quercus ilex
Holm oak
Yeuse; chêne yeuse; evergreen oak
Evergreen, leathery leaves are dark above and pale felted beneath. Margins range from nearly entire to spiny, especially on young shoots. Acorns sit in cups with small, appressed scales.
Dry Mediterranean woods and scrub; also occurs along the Atlantic coast and is planted elsewhere.
Quercus pubescens
Downy oak
Chêne blanc; white oak

A spreading oak with an irregular crown. Young twigs and leaf undersides are hairy; leaves have rounded lobes and a distinct stalk. Acorns are nearly sessile or shortly stalked. Dead leaves may persist in winter.
Warm slopes, often on limestone; frequent in southern France and locally farther north.
Populus nigra
Black poplar
Liard; peuplier d’Italie; Lombardy poplar

Finely toothed, triangular to diamond-shaped leaves and deeply fissured bark. Reddish male and female catkins occur on separate trees. Capsules release cottony seeds. The plate shows the spreading habit, rather than the Lombardy cultivar.
Riverbanks and floodplain woods; planted hybrid poplars can be difficult to distinguish.
Prunus padus
Bird cherry
Bois puant; putier; bird cherry
Long racemes of white flowers develop into small black drupes. Alternate, toothed leaves often have two glands near the top of the stalk. The bark bears conspicuous lenticels.
Cool woods, streamsides and valleys, especially in northern and eastern France and the mountains.
Malus sylvestris
Crab apple
Pommier des bois; wild apple

A small tree with sometimes spine-tipped short shoots. Mature leaves are almost hairless beneath; pink buds open into whitish flowers. Small apples retain their calyx. Hybrids with cultivated apples complicate identification.
Woodland edges and hedges, usually scattered across much of France.
Rhamnus cathartica
Purging buckthorn
Nerprun cathartique; common buckthorn
Shoots often end in a spine. Opposite to subopposite, sometimes alternate leaves are finely toothed, with a few strong curved veins. Greenish flowers have four parts; ripe drupes are black.
Hedges, scrub and open woodland, often on limestone.
Prunus mahaleb
St Lucie cherry
Bois de Sainte-Lucie; mahaleb cherry
A shrub or small tree with rounded, shiny, finely crenate leaves. Small clusters of fragrant white flowers produce pea-sized black drupes. Leaves are rounder than those of wild cherry.
Dry slopes, hedges and open woodland, mainly on limestone; frequent in southern and eastern France.
Matricaria chamomilla
German chamomile
Camomille allemande; Matricaria recutita; Chamomilla recutita; scented mayweed

An aromatic annual with leaves twice divided into very fine segments. Heads have white rays and a yellow disc; the receptacle becomes conical and is hollow, as shown in section. Fruits are small and ribbed.
Fields, waste ground and paths; frequency varies between regions.
Malva sylvestris
Common mallow
Grande mauve; mauve des bois; tall mallow

Rounded leaves have five to seven lobes and crenate margins. Five notched mauve petals bear darker veins; stamens are united into a column. The flat, wheel-shaped fruit is made of mericarps arranged around the centre.
Waste ground, roadsides and hedges, especially on enriched soils; widespread.
Potentilla reptans
Creeping cinquefoil
Quintefeuille; five-finger grass; creeping cinquefoil
Long runners root at their nodes. Long-stalked palmate leaves usually have five toothed leaflets. Solitary yellow flowers have five petals; many small achenes collect on the receptacle.
Grasslands, paths, ditches and compacted ground, often damp; very widespread.
Creeping indigo
Creeping indigo · Indigofera spicata

Prostrate to ascending perennial. Leaves usually bear seven leaflets inserted alternately along the rachis, broader near the tip. Dense racemes carry small pink to reddish pea flowers; short narrow pods turn downwards. Closely related Indigofera species require additional characters for identification.
Native across much of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Common in disturbed grassland, cultivated ground and fallows, often at moderate elevations.
Indigofera spicata
Douglas-fir
Oregon pine; sapin de Douglas; pin d’Oregon

Evergreen tree with soft, flat, singly attached needles and pointed buds. Hanging cones are unmistakable when their three-pointed bracts project beyond the rounded scales. Despite its common name, it is not a true fir.
Western North America, from British Columbia to Mexico, with coastal and inland populations. Widely planted in Europe.
Pseudotsuga menziesii
Northern red oak
Red oak; chêne rouge

Broad-crowned deciduous oak. Leaves have seven to eleven pointed, bristle-tipped lobes. Male flowers form slender hanging catkins; acorns sit in shallow saucer-like cups and mature in the second season.
Native to eastern North America. Introduced in Europe, including forest plantations; locally naturalized.
Quercus rubra
Catawba rhododendron
Mountain rosebay; Catawba rhododendron

Evergreen shrub with leathery elliptical leaves crowded near shoot tips. Large terminal clusters bear purple, broadly funnel-shaped flowers with five lobes, ten stamens and a marked upper lobe. Dry capsules split into valves.
Native to the southern Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States, on wooded slopes and rocky ridges.
Rhododendron catawbiense
Virginia rose
Virginia rose; rosier de Virginie
Suckering native rose with prickly stems and usually seven glossy, toothed leaflets. Open pink flowers have five petals and numerous stamens. Rounded red hips retain their sepals.
Eastern North America, from eastern Canada south into the United States, in open woods, coastal sites and thickets.
Rosa virginiana
Black-eyed Susan
Black-eyed Susan; rudbeckia

Hairy annual, biennial or short-lived perennial. Yellow ray florets surround a dark brown, raised central disc. Rough leaves are simple and usually alternate; the small dry fruits lack a conspicuous pappus.
Native to North America and now widespread in grasslands, roadsides and disturbed open ground; also introduced elsewhere.
Rudbeckia hirta
Large-leaved lupin
Bigleaf lupine; large-leaved lupine; lupin des jardins

Perennial with long-stalked palmate leaves, commonly bearing nine to seventeen narrow leaflets. Tall racemes carry blue to violet pea flowers. Hairy pods split at maturity. Many garden lupins are hybrids rather than this wild species.
Native to western North America, in moist meadows, stream margins and open woods. Introduced and sometimes invasive in Europe and other regions.
Lupinus polyphyllus
Sort by scientific name
Garden pea
Pisum sativum
Pea · Pois cultivé · Lathyrus oleraceus

Annual herb with weak stems supported by branched tendrils. Alternate leaves usually bear a few pairs of broad leaflets and end in tendrils; large leafy stipules flank the leaf base. Axillary flowers are white, pink or purple. The papilionaceous corolla has a standard, two wings and a keel of two petals; nine stamens are joined and one is free. The pod contains several seeds and can split along two sutures at maturity. Cultivars vary strongly in height, leaflets, pods and seed texture.

An ancient Old World crop now grown widely, especially in cool seasons on drained soils. The archive name Pisum sativum is retained for the living-tree link. Some current sources, including NC State, treat the same garden pea as Lathyrus oleraceus.
Climbing annual: leaves and tendrils arise along a flexible stem; flowers and developing pods are axillary.
Two pairs of oval leaflets, a branched terminal tendril and two broad stipules at the base. Cultivars may have more tendrils and fewer leaflets.
Papilionaceous flower: broad upper standard, two lateral wings and a lower keel. A smaller flower is shown separately.
Intact pod on the left; an opened pod on the right exposes seeds attached along one suture. Seed shape and colour vary by cultivar.
Asian rice
Oryza sativa
Cultivated rice · Riz cultivé · Paddy

Tufted annual grass with erect, jointed culms and long, narrow leaves. The sheath–blade junction bears a conspicuous membranous ligule and small ciliate auricles. A branched terminal panicle often bends as grains mature. Each spikelet contains one fertile floret, with six stamens and two feathery stigmas, above two reduced sterile lemmas. The grain is a caryopsis enclosed by the hardened lemma and palea: together these bracts form the husk removed during dehusking. Awns and grain shape vary; an awnless form is illustrated.
Asian domesticated cereal grown widely in warm regions. Often cultivated in flooded fields, but upland systems also exist. It is distinct from African cultivated rice, Oryza glaberrima.
Tuft of jointed culms, narrow leaves and loose branched panicles.
Long parallel-veined blade; inset shows the prominent pointed ligule and small hairy auricles at the top of the sheath.
Branched panicle with stalked spikelets; open fertile floret on the right, with six anthers and two feathery stigmas.
Main subject: dehusked caryopsis. Right: a separate husked spikelet above a small mature panicle. Husk and grain are different structures.
Tomato
Solanum lycopersicum
Tomate · Lycopersicon esculentum

Soft, hairy, branching plant, often sprawling unless supported. Alternate compound leaves carry lobed or toothed main leaflets with smaller leaflets between them. Yellow flowers have a fused corolla with pointed lobes; the elongated anthers form a cone around the style. The fruit is a berry with seeds in gel-filled locules. Cultivated forms differ greatly in growth habit, leaf shape, fruit colour and number of locules. The plate represents a round red, two-loculed tomato, not every cultivated variety.

American crop with ancestry in western South America and a long history of domestication. Now cultivated widely in warm seasons, under protection or in open fields. Often treated as an annual despite its perennial potential in frost-free conditions.
Branching, leafy stems with yellow flowering clusters and developing berries; an unsupported habit is represented.
Compound leaf: lobed principal leaflets, a terminal leaflet and small intercalary leaflets. The side shoot shows alternate insertion.
Continuous yellow corolla with five pointed lobes; elongated yellow anthers form a cone around the projecting style. Small flowering cluster at lower left.
Main subject: a round berry with persistent calyx. The separate transverse section shows two seed-bearing locules and their fleshy partition.
Eggplant
Solanum melongena
Aubergine · Brinjal

Upright branching herb or short-lived subshrub, commonly cultivated for one season. Broad alternate leaves have shallow lobes and often stellate hairs, especially beneath. Violet flowers have a fused corolla and yellow anthers opening by pores. The enlarged berry retains a prominent calyx; its spongy flesh contains many flattened seeds. Fruit shape, colour, size and prickliness vary markedly. The illustration uses a purple, elongated fruit and an unarmed calyx; white and rounded cultivars also exist.

Asian domesticated crop now cultivated widely in warm regions and protected cultivation. It is frost-sensitive and requires a warm growing season. The domesticated fruit range is much broader than a single purple cultivar.
Upright branching plant with broad leaves, violet flowers and hanging elongated berries.
Broad simple leaf with shallow lobes and reticulate venation. A stellate hair is enlarged separately at lower right.
Broad five-lobed violet corolla fused at the base; yellow, pore-bearing anthers encircle the style.
Purple elongated berry with a substantial persistent calyx. Longitudinal section at right shows pale flesh and numerous flattened seeds.
Black nightshade
Solanum nigrum
Morelle noire · European black nightshade

Usually annual, branching herb with simple ovate leaves, entire to irregularly toothed. Small, short-stalked cymes arise outside the leaf axils. White flowers have five spreading or reflexed lobes and a short yellow anther cone. Berries are commonly dark purple-black at maturity, with a small persistent calyx; the illustrated surface is only weakly shiny. This belongs to a complex of similar nightshades: fruit colour alone cannot distinguish the species. It is botanically distinct from deadly nightshade, Atropa belladonna.

Widespread in the Old World and introduced elsewhere, especially on disturbed, nutrient-rich soils, field edges, gardens and waste ground. The name has historically been applied broadly; identification within the black-nightshade group requires several characters together.
Branching annual with simple leaves, small white flowering cymes and clusters of dark berries outside the leaf axils.
Simple ovate leaf with a few shallow marginal teeth; some leaves are nearly entire. Small side shoot with alternate leaves.
Five white lobes of a fused corolla around a short cone of yellow anthers, with terminal pores. A small cyme is shown separately.
Enlarged dark berry with a small persistent calyx; right-hand inset shows several stalked berries on a short cyme. Colour alone is not diagnostic.
Olive
olive European olive oleaster

Evergreen tree with a gnarled trunk, opposite leathery leaves and silvery undersides. Small flowers have four lobes and two stamens. The olive is a drupe: its stone is the hardened inner fruit wall surrounding the seed. The plate represents a cultivated Mediterranean form; size and fruits vary among varieties.
Mediterranean region; the species also includes African and Asian populations. Cultivated in mild climates.
Twisted trunk and spreading grey-green crown.
Entire blade, silvery underside and opposite-leaved twig.
Four-lobed corolla, two stamens; panicle inset.
Ripe olive and longitudinal section showing flesh and stone.
Peach
peach nectarine

Small deciduous tree with long, toothed lanceolate leaves. Pink flowers with five petals and many stamens appear before or with the leaves. The peach is a drupe with a visible suture and deeply sculptured stone. The plate shows a fuzzy yellow-fleshed peach; smooth-skinned nectarines belong to the same species.
Native to China, long cultivated in warm temperate regions.
Open crown and shoots bearing elongated foliage.
Finely toothed lanceolate leaf; small glands near the petiole.
Five free pink petals, numerous stamens and central pistil.
Peach with suture, section and deeply grooved stone.
Olea europaea
Prunus persica
Punica granatum
Pomegranate
pomegranate balausta Punica granatum

Shrub or small tree with sometimes thorny shoots and small, entire, often opposite leaves. Flowers have a thick red tube, sepals, crumpled petals and many stamens. The pomegranate is a leathery berry; internal membranes divide groups of seeds with fleshy, juicy coverings.
Native to western Asia and long cultivated around the Mediterranean and in warm regions. Usually deciduous, sometimes more persistent in warm climates.
Multi-stemmed shrub with slender shoots and fruits crowned by the calyx.
Narrow, entire, glossy leaf; inset shows a pair of opposite leaves.
Six crumpled petals shown; side view of the fleshy floral tube and persistent sepals.
Whole pomegranate and schematic section: leathery rind, membranes and fleshy seeds.
Persea americana
Avocado
avocado alligator pear Persea americana

Tree with large, alternate, entire leaves. Small greenish flowers in panicles have six tepals, nine fertile stamens and three staminodes. Female and male function occur at different times. The avocado is a single-seeded berry, not a drupe with a stony pit; shape and skin vary among cultivars.
Native to Mexico and Central America; cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions. A green, pear-shaped fruit form is shown.
Broad-crowned tree; foliage visually gathers near shoot tips.
Elliptic leaf with a tapering tip, midrib and branching secondary veins.
Six tepals, nine stamens with four pollen sacs per anther and three staminodes; inset shows a panicle of small flowers.
Whole berry and longitudinal section: skin, flesh and a large seed without a stony endocarp.
Laurus nobilis
Bay laurel
bay laurel sweet bay culinary bay Laurus nobilis

Evergreen tree or shrub with alternate, leathery, aromatic leaves and entire, often wavy edges. Small umbels arise in leaf axils. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Only female plants bear fruit: small drupes that turn black at maturity. This is the bay used as a culinary herb.
Native to the Mediterranean basin; also cultivated in gardens in mild temperate regions.
Dense evergreen crown; natural habit differs from clipped topiary forms.
Lance-shaped blade with wavy, toothless edges; inset shows alternate leaves on a shoot.
Male flower with four tepals and twelve stamens in three whorls, the outer whorl without glands; female flower and umbel at separate scales.
Black drupe and longitudinal section with one seed; fruits occur on female plants.
Parsley
Petroselinum crispum
Parsley Petroselinum crispum
Biennial often harvested in its first year. Flowering stems and fruits normally develop in the second.
Mediterranean origin; cultivated in many regions.
Rosette followed by branched flowering stems.
Divided leaf; cultivars may be flat or curled.
Small greenish-yellow flowers in compound umbels.
Ribbed dry fruit composed of two mericarps.
Lovage
Levisticum officinale
Lovage Levisticum officinale
Tall aromatic perennial with divided leaves and a celery-like scent.
Europe and western Asia; cultivated and naturalized.
Robust branched stems; foliage on long petioles.
Compound leaf with broad toothed leaflets; subdivisions simplified.
Yellow flowers in compound umbels.
Ribbed dry fruit; two mericarps, each containing one seed.
Sweet marjoram
Origanum majorana
Sweet marjoram Origanum majorana
Frost-sensitive aromatic perennial often grown as an annual. Inflorescences bear overlapping bracts.
Eastern Mediterranean region; cultivated elsewhere.
Branched stems with opposite leaves.
Small oval, soft, slightly hairy leaf.
Small white or pink two-lipped corollas; inset shows clustered flowers and overlapping bracts.
Four nutlets; the calyx persists around the fruit.
Wild radish
Raphanus raphanistrum
Wild radish Raphanus raphanistrum
Annual field plant without a fleshy root. The fruit breaks between seeds rather than opening into two valves.
Europe and western Asia; naturalized elsewhere.
Upright stems and variable rosette.
Divided leaf with a large terminal lobe.
Four pale, sometimes yellow petals with darker veins.
Jointed fruit constricted between seeds; detached segment in the inset.
Watercress
Nasturtium officinale
Watercress Nasturtium officinale
Aquatic perennial with stems rooting at nodes. The genus Nasturtium belongs to Brassicaceae.
Europe and western Asia; widely naturalized.
Prostrate stems, nodal roots and emerging shoots.
Compound leaf; larger rounded terminal leaflet.
Small white four-petalled flowers.
Short silique opened to show two seed rows per chamber.
Banana
Musa acuminata
Musa acuminata

A giant herb: overlapping leaf sheaths make its pseudostem. Fruiting ends the life of that shoot, while the underground system produces replacements. Five fused tepals form a compound piece opposite one free tepal. Male flowers have five fertile stamens; female flowers have reduced stamens. Wild forms have seeded berries; many dessert cultivars have seedless fruits.
Native to tropical Asia; cultivated forms and hybrids are widespread. The plate shows a cultivated shoot.
Pseudostem, broad leaves, hanging fruits and a basal replacement sucker.
Simple blade with strong midrib, parallel lateral veins and natural tears.
Purple bracts uncover rows of pale tubular flowers.
Representative hand of cultivated berries; wild forms may contain hard seeds.
Date palm
Phoenix dactylifera
Phoenix dactylifera

A dioecious palm: male and female inflorescences occur on different plants. Stiff pinnate leaves have spiny basal leaflets. Usually one of the three carpels develops into a date. It is a one-seeded berry with a membranous inner fruit wall: its hard grooved seed is not a stone like a peach endocarp.
Arabian Peninsula to southern Pakistan according to Kew; widely cultivated in dry subtropical regions.
Upright pinnate crown, persistent leaf bases and a basal sucker.
Stiff pinnate frond with short sharp basal leaflets.
Branched panicle; the flowers of each sex belong to separate palms.
Oblong one-seeded berries and enlarged grooved seed, distinct from a drupe stone.
European pear
Pyrus communis
Pyrus communis

A deciduous rosaceous tree with alternate toothed leaves and white five-petalled flowers. The pear is a pome: fleshy accessory tissues surround the ovary-derived core. Cultivars vary greatly in shape, colour and size; the drawing shows a familiar necked form.
European and western Asian origins; widely cultivated in temperate orchards.
Rounded deciduous adult crown.
Oval blade, fine teeth and pinnate veins.
Five white petals, numerous stamens and five styles.
Necked pome and section showing the seed-bearing core.
Medlar
Mespilus germanica
Mespilus germanica

A small deciduous rosaceous tree. Solitary white flowers develop into brown pomes with an open end and five persistent sepals. The flesh includes accessory tissue surrounding the true fruit. Cultivated forms often have larger fruits than wild plants.
Southwest Asia and southeast Europe, despite the epithet germanica; cultivated since antiquity.
Small spreading deciduous tree.
Long simple blade with a softly hairy edge.
Solitary five-petalled white flower with numerous stamens.
Brown pome with an open depression and five persistent sepals.
Persian walnut
Juglans regia
Juglans regia

A broad-crowned deciduous tree with pinnate leaves, typically five to nine mostly entire leaflets. Male catkins and small female flowers occur on the same tree. The walnut is enclosed by a green husk; the hard shell surrounds a seed with folded cotyledons.
Eurasian origins and ancient cultivation; widely planted in temperate regions.
Broad spreading crown.
Odd-pinnate leaf with a large terminal leaflet.
Male catkin and enlarged female flower with two stigmatic lobes.
Green husk, hard grooved shell and folded kernel are separate structures.
Alpine currant
Ribes alpinum
Ribes alpinum

A deciduous shrub with small three-lobed leaves and green-yellow flowers. Usually dioecious, with male and female flowers on separate plants; only female plants produce red berries. Many ornamental selections sold for hedges are male.
Native to Europe and planted as a temperate ornamental shrub.
Dense shrub with many basal branches.
Small toothed three-lobed blade.
Short raceme of greenish flowers; the male flower is enlarged.
Red berries in a short raceme on a female plant.
Common juniper
Juniperus communis
Juniperus communis

An evergreen conifer with sharp leaves in whorls of three, each with a pale upper stomatal band. Usually cones of each sex occur on separate plants. The blue-black berry-like structure is a fleshy seed cone with fused scales, not an angiosperm berry.
Widespread in northern temperate regions; forms range from prostrate mats to small trees.
Representative upright conical form.
Three leaves per whorl, with pale stomatal bands.
Pollen and female cones, without petals.
Fleshy blue-black cones and cut cone with seeds.
Stone pine
Pinus pinea
Pinus pinea

An evergreen Mediterranean conifer with an umbrella-shaped adult crown and needles paired in fascicles. Woody cones enclose large pine nuts: these are seeds, not botanical nuts. The woody cone protects its seeds with scales, rather than an ovary-derived fruit wall.
Mediterranean region and warm temperate plantings. Young crowns differ from the adult umbrella illustrated.
Adult umbrella crown and tall branching trunk.
Two long needles share a basal fascicle sheath.
Pollen cones and young seed cone without petals.
Broad woody cone with thick scales; pine nuts are seeds.
Common toadflax
Linaria vulgaris
Linaria vulgaris

A rhizomatous perennial with narrow leaves, alternate above but sometimes whorled below, and yellow two-lipped flowers. The orange palate closes the flower entrance; a long backward spur stores nectar. Capsules open by teeth near the apex, releasing flattened seeds.
Native to Eurasia; introduced in other temperate regions.
Upright stems with narrow leaves and terminal flowers.
Narrow entire blade on an alternate leafy shoot.
Raised orange palate and long nectar spur in side view.
Dry capsule with apical teeth, not a silique.
Small pasque flower
Pulsatilla pratensis
Pulsatilla pratensis

A hairy grassland perennial with finely divided basal leaves and a nodding cylindrical flower. Usually six petaloid perianth segments have recurved tips. After flowering, the axis elongates and each achene keeps a long feathery style, aiding dispersal. These tails are not a composite-flower pappus.
Central and northern Europe to Central Asia; especially sunny dry grasslands and forest margins.
Nodding flower above divided leaves; fruiting axis shown separately elongated.
Finely divided hairy basal leaf.
Six free petaloid segments surrounding many stamens; side and end views.
Achene with a long feathery persistent style; fruit cluster inset.
Multiflora rose
Rosa multiflora
Rosa multiflora

A many-flowered shrub with arching prickly stems and pinnate leaves. Fringed stipules at the leaf base distinguish it from many other roses. Small white flowers form clusters. Red hips are fleshy accessory receptacles enclosing multiple one-seeded achenes.
East Asian origins; cultivated and introduced widely, sometimes spreading vigorously.
Arching prickly shrub with clustered flowers.
Seven representative toothed leaflets and fringed stipules at the petiole base.
Cluster of small five-petalled white flowers.
Small red hips containing achenes, rather than fleshy seeds.
Beach pea
Lathyrus japonicus
Lathyrus japonicus

A perennial coastal legume spreading from underground axes. Broad paired leaflets end in a tendril; stipules occur at the leaf base. Purple pea flowers form short stalked clusters, followed by flat pods. The epithet japonicus does not restrict the species to Japan.
Northern temperate coasts, including Europe, Asia and North America; especially sandy or shingle shores.
Spreading perennial with leafy shoots.
Eight representative broad leaflets and a terminal tendril.
Stalked group of purple pea flowers.
Flattened pod with a row of seeds.
Bur medick
Medicago minima
Medicago minima

A small hairy annual with trifoliate leaves and tiny yellow pea flowers. Its pod coils tightly into a spiral with hooked marginal spines, making a burr. It remains closed at maturity: being a legume does not require every pod to split open.
European, Mediterranean and western Asian origins; introduced in other dry temperate regions.
Low spreading hairy annual.
Three small toothed leaflets.
Tiny yellow pea flower, enlarged for comparison.
Closed spiral pod with hooked marginal spines.
Sweet potato
Ipomoea batatas
sweetpotato; sweet potato vine

Trailing tropical perennial morning-glory with alternate heart-shaped or palmately lobed leaves and funnel-shaped flowers. Its edible storage organs are enlarged roots, unlike the stem tubers of the unrelated common potato (Solanum tuberosum). Leaf shape varies among cultivars.
Tropical American origin; cultivated widely in warm regions.
Creeping vine with storage roots beneath the crown.
Alternate heart-shaped leaf with radiating basal veins; lobed forms also occur.
Funnel-shaped five-lobed corolla, usually pale lavender or white.
Enlarged storage root, not a stem tuber; capsule production varies in cultivation.
Japanese star anise
Illicium anisatum
Japanese anise tree; poisonous star anise

Evergreen East Asian shrub or small tree with alternate glossy leaves, creamy many-petalled flowers and a star-shaped aggregate of follicles. This species is poisonous. Its dried fruit can resemble culinary Chinese star anise in trade; a picture or casual visual inspection cannot authenticate processed spice. Never use this plate to identify food.
Native to Japan, Korea and Taiwan; cultivated elsewhere.
Evergreen woody plant with alternate leaves and axillary flowers.
Glossy simple elliptic leaf with entire, slightly wavy margins.
Creamy flower with numerous petal-like tepals.
Poisonous star-shaped aggregate fruit; never use as a spice or identify food from this image.
Bracken fern
Pteridium aquilinum
bracken; eagle fern

Rhizomatous fern whose large triangular fronds divide two or three times. Sori form a nearly continuous line along fertile segment margins, protected by the rolled-under leaf edge. It has no flowers, fruits or seeds. Bracken contains toxic compounds; do not treat it as food.
Nearly cosmopolitan in temperate and tropical regions; open woodland, heaths and disturbed ground.
Large single frond rising from a long creeping rhizome.
Triangular blade divided two or three times into many pinnules.
No flowers: this fern reproduces by spores.
Marginal sori and sporangia; no fruit or seed.
Dawn redwood
Metasequoia glyptostroboides
Dawn redwood; water fir

A large deciduous conifer from a restricted area of central China. Its fine feathery branchlets and leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, unlike the alternate sprays of coast redwood. Small pollen cones and rounded seed cones are separate reproductive structures; the seed cones hang from short shoots.
Native to central China; widely planted elsewhere as an ornamental tree.
Tall, straight-trunked, conical tree with soft deciduous foliage and reddish-brown bark.
Flattened, feathery branchlets carry opposite pairs of short linear leaves; both leaves and lateral shoots are deciduous.
A wind-pollinated conifer: small male pollen cones occur in clusters; no petals are present.
Rounded woody seed cones mature on hanging stalks and release small winged seeds.
Passion fruit
Passiflora edulis
Passion fruit; purple granadilla; maracujá

A vigorous perennial liana with axillary tendrils and usually three-lobed leaves. Its solitary flowers have five sepals, five petals, a conspicuous many-ranked corona and a raised central reproductive column. The berry varies from yellow to purple according to cultivated form; do not use fruit colour alone to identify it.
Native to Brazil through Paraguay and northeastern Argentina; cultivated and naturalised throughout warm regions.
Climbing evergreen or seasonally deciduous vine supported by simple tendrils.
Alternate, usually three-lobed leaves have serrate edges; the leaf stalk commonly bears paired glands.
A large solitary flower has a white perianth, purple-and-white filamentous corona and five stamens on an androgynophore.
A many-seeded berry with a leathery rind and juicy arils; mature rind may be purple or yellow.
Lychee
Litchi chinensis
Lychee; litchi

An evergreen subtropical tree in the soapberry family. Its paripinnate leaves have glossy upper surfaces and pale undersides. Flowers are small and lack petals; the rounded fruit has a thin, scaly pink-red rind and a translucent aril surrounding the seed.
Native from southern China through mainland Southeast Asia to Malaysia, Borneo and the Philippines; widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
Evergreen, round-crowned tree, usually branched from a short trunk.
Alternate paripinnate leaves bear opposite to subopposite entire leaflets, glossy above and paler beneath.
Tiny apetalous flowers with a short calyx and several stamens are borne in terminal branched panicles.
A globose to obovoid indehiscent fruit has a thin scaly rind and a seed completely enclosed by a translucent aril.
Unarmed pitcher plant
Nepenthes inermis
Unarmed pitcher plant; Nepenthes inermis

A Sumatran highland pitcher plant that climbs or grows among mossy forest vegetation. Its leaves end in tendrils bearing distinctive upper pitchers: narrow below, funnel-shaped above, and with a nearly absent peristome. The pitchers are modified leaves; the actual flowers occur separately in a raceme.
Endemic to montane western Sumatra, Indonesia.
Slender climbing or scrambling tropical perennial, often epiphytic in humid montane forest.
Alternate simple leaves have a prolonged midrib forming a tendril that terminates in a pitcher trap.
Small unisexual flowers occur in a separate raceme; flowers are not formed inside the pitchers.
A dry capsule splits into valves to release seeds; the pitcher is a leaf structure, not a fruit.
Elephant’s foot
Pachypodium rosulatum
Elephant’s foot; Madagascar pachypodium

A Madagascan succulent shrub with a swollen water-storing stem and spiny ascending branches. Narrow leaves cluster near branch tips, and yellow flowers have a long narrow tube. The species complex is variable and divided into several subspecies; this plate shows a representative caudiciform form.
Endemic to Madagascar in seasonally dry rocky habitats.
Succulent shrub with a large bottle-shaped caudex, branching above the base; height and shape vary among subspecies.
Simple narrow leaves form terminal rosettes on branches and may be shed in the dry season.
Yellow five-lobed flowers have a conspicuous tubular corolla, often with darker longitudinal markings in some subspecies.
Paired narrow follicles split at maturity and release seeds, often with a tuft of hairs.
Kratom tree
Mitragyna speciosa
Kratom; ketum; Mitragyna

A tropical evergreen tree in the coffee family. Opposite broad leaves have curved secondary veins and small domatia in vein axils; rounded heads of many tiny flowers occur near branch tips. This description is botanical and does not imply that any plant part is safe to consume.
Native from mainland Southeast Asia through Malesia to New Guinea, often in wet lowland and riverine habitats.
Medium to large evergreen tree, sometimes with a buttressed base, growing in wet lowland forests.
Opposite, petiolate, entire leaves have prominent curved veins and small domatia in some vein axils.
Numerous minute flowers are packed into round terminal or near-terminal heads.
The small dry capsules mature within a globose flower head and split to release seeds.
Autumn narcissus
Narcissus serotinus
Autumn narcissus; late narcissus

A small autumn-flowering bulbous geophyte of the western Mediterranean. One white flower bears six tepals and a very short yellow corona with a divided rim, among the smallest coronas in the genus. Historical records farther east may refer to other autumn-flowering Narcissus species, so range matters for identification.
Native to the western Mediterranean, including the Iberian Peninsula and Morocco.
Small bulbous herb; flowers appear in autumn, with narrow leaves often developing later.
Narrow, linear basal leaves are shorter than or similar in length to the flowering scape.
Usually one white flower has six spreading tepals and a very small yellow, six-lobed corona.
An ovoid three-lobed capsule contains numerous seeds.
Powder-puff cactus
Mammillaria bocasana
Powder-puff cactus; woolly nipple cactus

A small clustered cactus native to northeastern Mexico. Rounded stems bear tubercles with abundant fine white radial spines and a smaller number of stronger central spines, sometimes hooked. It has no true leaves: the conspicuous structures are spines arising from areoles.
Native to northeastern Mexico, extending south to Jalisco, in dry scrub and desert habitats.
Low, slowly clustering succulent with globose stems only a few centimetres across.
True leaves are absent; each tubercle bears an areole with fine hair-like radial spines and usually a few longer central spines.
Small pale cream to pink flowers form a ring near the stem apex.
Small red, elongated berries emerge among the tubercles after flowering.
Western bog laurel
Kalmia microphylla
Western bog laurel; little-leaf laurel

A low evergreen North American shrub of wet meadows, bog margins and alpine habitats. Opposite leathery leaves and terminal rose-purple flowers help distinguish it from related Kalmia. Like other laurels in the family, it is toxic if eaten.
Western North America from California and the Rocky Mountains north into Canada and Alaska.
Low spreading to upright shrub, about 5–80 cm high, often rooted in acidic wet ground.
Small opposite leathery leaves are elliptic to lance-shaped, with entire margins often slightly rolled under.
Rose-purple, saucer-shaped flowers occur singly or in terminal clusters; ten stamens are held in petal sacs before anthesis.
A small five-celled capsule releases tiny winged seeds.
Bristlecone hemlock
Nothotsuga longibracteata
Bristlecone hemlock; long-bracted hemlock

A rare evergreen conifer endemic to southern China. Its needles spread radially rather than forming a flat two-ranked spray, and its nearly upright seed cones carry conspicuous bracts extending beyond the scales. Older floras may list it as Tsuga longibracteata; the accepted genus here follows POWO.
Endemic to montane southern China, mainly at low to middle elevations.
Narrow evergreen tree with horizontal branches and a dense conical crown.
Short linear needles are radially arranged around the shoots, with stomatal lines on both surfaces.
Small pollen cones occur in clusters; this conifer has no petals or true flowers.
Ovoid seed cones are approximately erect; their elongated, three-lobed bracts protrude beyond the woody scales.
Azobé
Lophira alata
Azobé; red ironwood; ekki

A very large West and Central African rainforest tree, known for exceptionally dense timber. Its leathery simple leaves have pinnate venation, and small flowers are borne in terminal panicles. The fruit is a nut accompanied by two greatly enlarged, unequal sepals that aid wind dispersal; these are not fruit wings in the samara sense.
Native from West Tropical Africa east to Uganda, mainly in humid forests; assessed as Vulnerable by IUCN.
Large evergreen rainforest tree with a tall straight trunk and broad crown.
Alternate, simple, leathery oblong leaves have entire margins and a conspicuous midrib with pinnate lateral veins.
Small white, scented flowers with five petals and numerous stamens occur in terminal panicles.
A hard nut is accompanied by two unequal enlarged sepals, forming one long and one shorter wing-like lobe.
Guernsey lily
Nerine sarniensis
Guernsey lily; blood lily

A bulbous South African geophyte with a distinctive seasonal cycle: scarlet flowers emerge on a leafless scape in autumn, while strap-shaped leaves develop later. The strongly recurved tepals and projecting stamens make the flower recognizable. “Guernsey lily” is a common name, not its native range.
Native to the winter-rainfall region of the Western Cape, South Africa; naturalised in a few other places.
Bulbous perennial, dormant in summer; the autumn flowering scape normally appears before the leaves.
Narrow strap-like leaves emerge after flowering and persist through the cooler growing season.
An umbel bears bright red flowers with six narrow, strongly recurved tepals and long stamens.
A three-lobed capsule follows flowering and releases dark seeds.
Erect prickly pear
Opuntia stricta
Erect prickly pear; common pest pear

A spreading coastal prickly pear native to the southeastern United States and nearby Mexico. Its flattened green pads are modified stems, not leaves; areoles bear glochids and sometimes longer spines. Yellow flowers are followed by fleshy red-purple fruits. Opuntia species hybridise and vary, so pad shape alone is not a secure field identification.
Native from the southeastern United States through eastern and southern Mexico; widely introduced and invasive in some regions.
Low to spreading succulent shrub composed of flattened cladodes, often forming dense colonies.
True leaves are minute and short-lived; the persistent flat pads are stem segments with areoles and glochids.
Large yellow flowers arise singly from the margins or upper portions of mature pads.
A fleshy, often reddish-purple berry-like fruit follows flowering; glochids may remain on its surface.
Purple passionflower
Passiflora incarnata
Purple passionflower; maypop

A perennial North American climbing subshrub with tendrils and deeply three-lobed leaves. Its large flower has white to pale-lavender sepals and petals, a striking purple-and-white filamentous corona and a central reproductive column. The yellow-green berry is often called a maypop; cultivated passion fruit is usually P. edulis, a different species.
Native to the central and eastern United States and Bermuda; introduced and naturalised elsewhere.
Climbing perennial with herbaceous shoots, tendrils and rhizomes that can spread underground.
Alternate leaves are deeply three-lobed with toothed edges; axillary tendrils aid climbing.
Large solitary flowers have five sepals, five petals, several concentric corona rows, five stamens and three styles.
An oval yellow-green berry contains many dark seeds, each surrounded by a pulpy aril.
